a: in Idumea
p: Alexandrinus says Judas fought Esau's people "in Judea"; Sinaiticus and Venetus say "in Idumea".

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus (ℵ, 300s AD) and Codex Venetus (V, 700s AD), in Swete's notes; Latin Vulgate; KJV
readings.orig: Ιουδαια] Ιδουμαια ℵV; Latin in Idumæa
readings.plain: in Idumea

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: in Judea

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. The descendants of Esau lived in Idumea (5:65), and the two names differ by a few letters in Greek, so a copyist could easily write the familiar "Judea". Sinaiticus, Venetus and the Latin agree on Idumea, and so does the parallel in Josephus.

a: kept Israel hemmed in
p: The first hand of Sinaiticus has "Amalek"; the KJV has a place, "Gael".

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete; Venetus; Sinaiticus as corrected by ℵ¹ (a correction later undone)
readings.plain: kept Israel hemmed in

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus, first hand (ℵ*), in Swete's notes
readings.orig: Ισραηλ] Αμαληκ ℵ* Ισλ ℵ¹ (Αμ. uncis incl ℵ¹ improb ℵc.a c.b)
readings.plain: kept Amalek hemmed in

readings.w: King James Version (1611); its source is not identified, and Swete's apparatus has no such Greek
readings.plain: kept Gael under siege

why: Israel makes sense: the Idumeans pressed the Jews. Sinaiticus' first scribe wrote "Amalek", perhaps thinking of Esau's descendant Amalek (Genesis 36:12), and the corrector ℵ¹ bracketed it and wrote "Israel", a change that the later correctors ℵc.a and ℵc.b rejected. The KJV's "Gael" is a place-name not found in Swete's manuscripts.

a: Jazer
p: Alexandrinus writes the town's name Jazen; Sinaiticus and Venetus have Jazer, the town of Numbers 21:32.

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Venetus, in Swete's notes; KJV (Jazar)
readings.plain: Jazer

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.plain: Jazen

readings.w: Latin Vulgate
readings.plain: Gazer

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. Jazer was an Ammonite border town east of the Jordan (Numbers 21:32; Joshua 13:25), which fits a campaign against the Ammonites. Alexandrinus' final n is a common slip for r in copying names.

a: the gate of Ptolemais
p: Alexandrinus says "the towns of Ptolemais"; Sinaiticus, Venetus, the Latin and the KJV say "the gate".

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Venetus, in Swete's notes; Latin Vulgate (its 5:21); KJV

readings.plain: the towns of Ptolemais

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. "Gate" (pylēs) and "towns" (poleōn) look alike in Greek. Ptolemais was a single city, and chasing an enemy to a city's gate is a common picture; three witnesses agree on it.

a: Chaspho, Maked
p: Alexandrinus spells the names Kasphor and Makeb here, and Chasphoth and Maked at 5:36.

why: The manuscripts spell these unknown towns of Gilead in many ways, even within one manuscript (Alexandrinus has Chasphoth at 5:36). The Plain English Translation uses one form for each town in both verses: Chaspho, close to Sinaiticus' first hand, and Maked, which Alexandrinus itself has at 5:36. The towns are the same either way.

p: The Latin and the KJV name the town Maspha (Mizpah).

p: The spies say "around you" in Alexandrinus, "around us" in the other manuscripts and the KJV.

why: Both make sense; "you" fits spies reporting to Judas. In Greek the two words differ by one letter and were often confused.

a: have gathered to him
p: Alexandrinus says the nations gathered "to them"; Sinaiticus and the Latin say "to him", that is, to Timothy.

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. "To them" has no clear antecedent in the scouts' report; "to him" points back to Timothy, who had gathered the army (5:37).

p: Alexandrinus says his people went "in front of him", which cannot be right if he crossed first.

a: Joseph son of Zechariah and Azariah
p: Alexandrinus says "Joseph son of Zechariah, and Zechariah"; Venetus, the Latin and the KJV have Azariah, as in 5:18 and 5:60.

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. The two commanders are Joseph and Azariah in 5:18 and 5:60; a copyist's eye picked up "Zechariah" from the father's name just before.

a: They wanted to do brave deeds, and they went out to battle without thinking it through
t: Who wanted to do brave deeds?
p: Alexandrinus says "he" wanted to do brave deeds; Sinaiticus' first hand and the Latin make it the priests.

why: Alexandrinus' singular ("he") must mean each priest, unless it means Judas, which the book would never say of its hero. Sinaiticus' first hand and the Latin have the plural, which the Plain English Translation follows for clarity. The meaning is the same either way, so the Plain English Translation treats this as a matter of wording, not a departure in sense.

a: Eleazar Avaran
p: Alexandrinus and the KJV call him Savaran; Sinaiticus Auran (as Josephus has it), Venetus Avaran, as in 2:5; the Latin "son of Saura".

why: Here the Plain English Translation departs from Alexandrinus. In 2:5 the brother is called Avaran. Sinaiticus and Venetus have the long form of his name, Eleazaros ho Auaran; the sigma of Alexandrinus' ho Sauaran is probably the final -s of Eleazaros, which stuck to the surname when the name was shortened to Eleazar. The Latin turned the surname into a father's name.

readings.plain: "O Lord, when King Sennacherib's men blasphemed you

readings.w: King James Version (1611); its source is not identified, and Swete's apparatus has no such Greek
readings.en: O Lord, when they that were sent from the king of the Assyrians blasphemed
readings.plain: "O Lord, when the men sent by the king of the Assyrians blasphemed

why: The Greek names neither God nor the king; 1 Maccabees avoids naming God, and the readers knew the story. The Latin and the KJV fill in what the story implies.

a: no grain, weapons or money shall be given
p: Sinaiticus, Venetus, the Latin and the KJV add "ships", as in 8:26.

readings.w: Codex Alexandrinus (A, 400s AD), as printed by Swete
readings.en: grain, weapons, money shall not be given
readings.plain: no grain, weapons or money shall be given

readings.w: Codex Sinaiticus and Codex Venetus, in Swete's notes; Latin Vulgate; KJV
readings.orig: αργυριον] + πλοα ℵV [sic, for πλοῖα]; Latin triticum, arma, pecunia, naves
readings.plain: no grain, weapons, money or ships shall be given

why: Rome had a navy and the Jews did not, so the Jews' promise in 8:26 includes ships and Rome's here may not have. The other witnesses may have made the two lists match. Alexandrinus is kept.
